blocks.text: Spacecraft (or craft for short) are aircraft-like small vehicles that can be launched from hangars on larger ships. They can perform a number of roles, including scouting, electronic warfare, anti-missile and anti-craft fire, and anti-ship strikes. Their ability to receive orders after launch makes them more flexible than other tools such as cruise missiles.

Craft are controlled similarly to ships, but with context-sensitive actions depending on the item the cursor is pointing at when right-clicked. Where multiple valid controls exist, additional commands may be accessed by holding Shift.

rows: Opens the dial widget to allow movement. Holding Shift will allow placement of waypoints as normal. May also be opened via the ship 'move to position' hotkey.
Craft will move into a holding pattern moving around the target ship. If it has anti-craft/missile armaments, it will be slaved to the ship's PD controller and will attack incoming threats.
Craft will line up and attempt to land on the target ship. It will orbit the ship until a landing pad is free and the ship is within flight quarters speeds.
Craft will move into a holding pattern moving around the target craft. If it has anti-craft/missile armaments, it will be slaved to the craft's PD controller and will attack incoming threats.
Craft will join with the target craft/flight to form a unified flight.

Craft will move towards the target ship and attempt to attack it with appropriate weapons. Behaviour is dependent on the craft's set stance toggles. Craft will automatically deauthorise weapons that cannot harm ships when given an attack ship order.
Craft will move into range of the target with its module and enter a holding pattern, attempting to keep the target jammed/illuminated/scanned.

Craft will move toward the target craft/flight and attempt to attack it with appropriate weapons. Behaviour is dependent on the craft's set stance toggles. Craft will automatically deauthorise weapons that cannot harm craft when given an attack craft order.

Craft flights will fly in a cross-shaped pattern, perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Craft flights will fly in an echelon (diagonal line) shaped pattern.

blocks.text: Craft not in formation will speed up faster than their top speed in attempt to form up; this includes when swapping formation.

Craft will only dogfight with guns if the enemy is within about 1 km beyond gun range, or they were already in gun range when the attack order was issued.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › Craft guns

rows: RS-35 Halberd nose and mission package

blocks.text: "Closes to" is the range craft approach to before firing. Once a target is in reach, a gun fires out to the full range of its ammunition.
"Spread at 1 km" is the width of the firing cone 1 km out, as shown in the craft editor. The Barracuda's rocket pods spread 10 times wider than the Sturgeon's.
The Halberd's 35mm guns are turrets: 90°/s traverse, ±20° elevation. The nose turret is limited to ±90° traverse; the mission turret has no limit.
A gun fires only when all of these hold:
the predicted lead point is lined up with the barrel, within 10–60 m depending on the gun;
the lead point is within range, and no closer than 5% of the ammunition's range: 88 m for 20mm and 35mm guns, 150 m for rockets, 360 m for the 100mm pods and 400 m for the coilgun;
no terrain or friendly ship is in the way.
Fixed guns need the whole craft pointed at the lead point.
Against ships, guns aim at a random point on the hull, picked again on each attack run, unless the ATGT setting selects a subsystem. Against craft and missiles they aim at the centre.
The 20mm Gun never fires at ships.
Craft dogfight with guns when the enemy craft is within gun range + 1 km, when they launched without missiles or rockets, or when RANGE is set to GUN.
On a gun run, craft match the target's speed.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › Craft Radar Stats

blocks.text: Craft radars are broadly very similar, though they have some small differences.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › How facing changes the return

blocks.text: Ships use a fixed table of 162 directions. Their displayed signature is the maximum, and most angles are lower.
Craft and missiles use a radar box fixed to the airframe. Their radar cross-section (RCS) is the area of that box as the radar sees it: each face counts by how squarely it faces the radar.[4]
The return is smallest nose-on or tail-on.
It is largest when the radar sees the side, top and nose at once, for example with the craft banked 45°. That happens about 57–63° off the nose for craft, and 65–75° for missiles.
In level flight the largest return is only 1.24–1.35× the side-on value for craft, and 1.07–1.20× for missiles.
The displayed craft signature is the side-on value.
For craft, the banked peak is 1.6–1.7× the displayed value, and nose-on is 0.73–0.91×.
For missiles, the banked peak is about 1.5× the side-on value, and nose-on is 0.38–0.66×.
Pitch, yaw and roll all change the return, because the box turns with the airframe.
The same value is used by search radars on ships and craft, by track accuracy, and by missile seekers. A ship holding a fire-control lock reuses the last value computed for that target.
Detection range grows with the fourth root of the RCS: doubling the RCS gives about 19% more range.
A craft seen nose-on is detected at 0.82–0.86× the range of its peak angle.
A missile seen nose-on is detected at 0.71–0.81× that range.

blocks.text: † The radar's maximum range is reached first. The game adds half the target's length to the maximum, so these targets are seen up to 55 m beyond it.

Craft radars reach 3 km (fighters) or 4 km (Halberd, Claymore, Sturgeon). A 3 km craft radar sees every craft out to its full range. A 4 km one falls slightly short against the Tanto, Pike and Claymore from some angles (3.7–4.0 km).
Against small missiles craft radars fall well short. A 4 km craft radar sees a Balestra-size missile at 2.0 / 2.6 / 2.8 km.
The E-44 Sundial's 10 km radar sees a Tanto at 8.5 / 8.7 / 9.95 km.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › Signature modifiers

blocks.text: Craft modifiers multiply: the craft's own stat × the flight's stat.
The flight-size values are the defaults in the game code. The values set for flights in the game data were not read.
If a flight has two modifiers, the smaller one counts at only about 37% of its value. A flight of 6–10 craft with radars off is +13%, not +10%.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › Craft countermeasures

blocks.text: A pattern is a string of chaff packets dropped from under a craft as it flies. The packets form one decoy cloud that traces the craft's path. Every craft has a Countermeasures socket that holds one of three launchers.
The second to fourth rows use the in-game stat names. Each shot drops one chaff packet. The game shows the High-Coherence spacing as 0.13 s; the exact value is 0.125 s.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › The chaff cloud

blocks.text: Packets drop 8 m below the craft and stay where they were dropped.
The cloud is one box around all live packets, padded by 10 m.
Length = craft speed × 2.25 s + 10 m (2.375 s for High-Coherence).
Thickness is at least 10 m. Craft jink while evading, which makes it thicker.
The cloud is full size from the last packet until 6 s. After 6 s it shrinks from the oldest end. It is gone at 8.25 s (8.375 s for High-Coherence).
The box is aligned to the map axes, not to the flight path. A trail flown diagonally across the map makes a larger box.

Its radar return is the area of the box as the radar sees it, times the multiplier. Seen side-on, a cloud returns its length × 10 m. Seen end-on, it returns at least 100 m² (200 m² for High-Coherence).
Its wake can be seen from all directions. A craft's own wake is strength 1 before modifiers and can only be seen within 75° of its tail.
It fools active radar, semi-active radar and wake seekers.
It does nothing against EO (electro-optical), passive radar or home-on-jam seekers. Missiles with an EO validator reject it.
It is not flagged as a point-defense target, so seekers set to ignore small targets still see it.
It cannot be shot down.
Pattern counts refill when the craft is relaunched.
Cruise speeds are from the spaceframe data. The wiki's craft table lists the Tanto, Barracuda and Pike at 1 m/s faster.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › When craft drop countermeasures

blocks.text: Craft drop countermeasures only while evading. An evasion starts when a missile is 5 s or less from impact (3 s or less with DFTAC OUT-G).
Each evasion drops at most one pattern, at its start. An evasion lasts up to 6 s.
When a different threat becomes the most urgent, a new evasion starts and drops a new pattern. A staggered salvo can use up several patterns.
A new pattern can't start until 2.5 s after the previous one began.
Craft know the incoming missile's seeker types without needing intel on it.
Evasion manoeuvres:

Notch: fly straight away from the missile for 1.5 s (2.5 s when the Halberd, Barracuda, Pike or Tanto notches against a seeker that is neither radar nor wake), then turn across its path, presenting a side profile in the hopes that seduced missiles will be unable to re-acquire[5]. The pattern drops at the start, while the craft is still flying away, so the trail is usually not side-on to the missile.
Scoot: turn onto a new, partly random course. The code tilts the direction to the missile by angles fixed to the map, so the course is not at a set angle to the missile.
Flee: fly straight away from the threat.
Jink: turn hard across the line to the threat. DFTAC OUT-G uses this against missiles.
Sweeping turn: turn around to face an attacker behind the craft.
Against gunfire from enemy craft:
The Halberd, Barracuda and Pike jink when two or more enemy guns are firing at them and the fire is 1 s from impact. Two guns on one enemy craft count as two.
The Tanto turns to face an attacker behind it under the same conditions, and its flight-mates are ordered to attack the shooter.
The Claymore, Sturgeon and Sundial flee when gunfire is 5 s from impact.
The same gun can't trigger another evasion until 12 s after the last one started.
None of these drop a pattern unless CMSR is set to ALL.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Craft Stats › High-Coherence and proximity fuzes

blocks.text: The High-Coherence cloud is solid to missile proximity fuzes.
A missile with a blast-fragmentation warhead has a 33% chance to detonate on the cloud each time its fuze touches it.
The only stock missile with an older-style proximity warhead, the FBU-15 bomb, is set to detonate on ships only, so it ignores the cloud.
Flak shells don't detect the cloud.
Standard and High-Capacity clouds don't set off fuzes.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Designing Craft › Launch and Recovery Sequence

blocks.text: Select Armaments -> Give Flight Sortie Command -> Arm on a pad or strikedown slot -> Launch -> pad stays busy for Deck Traversal Time -> Return -> Land -> Disarm while that pad spends its traversal time -> Stored -> Repair if a repair slot is free

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Designing Craft › Arming/disarming time

blocks.text: A Craft must be readied before it can sortie from a carrier. This includes loading fuel and ordinance onto the Craft. The duration to complete the readying operation depends on the the size and ammunition loaded the time that. This ranges from arming a vehicle without armaments with virtually little to no time to a significant amount of time such as your bombers.
When a craft returns, any unspent ordinance must be removed and returned to stores, this occurs before the craft is repaired.
Some Carriers have bonuses to Arming Speed, and the Gear Deck Locker can increase the speed as well.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Designing Craft › Deck Traversal Time

blocks.text: Deck Traversal Time is a pad turnaround. After a craft launches, or after it is recovered and stored, that pad cannot take another craft until the traversal time has elapsed. It does not delay the craft that is launching.
Recovering a craft also ties up the pad for the deck traversal time (after a short close delay). The craft is stored and starts disarming while that pad wait is still running.
Some Carriers have bonuses to Arming Speed, and the Flight Deck Traversal System can increase the speed as well.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Designing Craft › Craft Repair

blocks.text: Damaged craft are repaired after disarming, one per free repair slot. A craft that is repairing, or still waiting for a slot, can still be launched, and it sorties with whatever damage it still has.

The number of slots that a craft can repair at is equal to the number of Spacecraft Repair Slots on the selected Hull. Carrier Hulls like the Levy, Moorline and Journeyman each have 1 slot and can only repair one craft at a time. Non-carrier hulls have no slots and cannot repair craft by default.
Each Spacecraft Repair Station adds one repair slot on top of the hull base. For example, a Marauder with 1 Spacecraft Repair Station can repair 1 Barracuda Strike Fighter at a time.

sections.heading: Spacecraft Mechanics › Designing Craft › Preflight Slots

blocks.text: The number of slots that a carrier can arm craft is equal to the number of small and large launch pads on the selected Carrier. For example the Levy has 2 Large and 4 small pads, and the Journeyman 2 Large and 2 Small pads, while the number of pads for the Moorline is directly related to the number of Bank Hangar's installed. Both the Journeyman and Moorline can install additional small mounted hangars for additional size 1 preflight slots.

This number can be increased with Spacecraft Strikedown Stations, this will allow additional craft to be armed in addition to the ones that can be armed on the launch pads. Craft armed there move onto a launch pad as soon as one is free, which is after the previous launch or recovery finishes its deck-traversal wait, and they keep the arming progress already made. For example, a Levy or Journeyman with 2 Spacecraft Strikedown Stations can arm a 4 wing Claymore Torpedo Flight at the same time and launch them much faster than they would otherwise.
